01 — Sampling

The model never picks a word. It picks from a distribution.

Prompt — “the sky at sunset turns…” Balanced
1.00

Temperature divides every score before the probabilities are worked out. Low temperature makes the leader run away with it; high temperature levels the field until nonsense gets a turn.

01 — Sampling

Two ways to cut the tail off

 

Top-p · counts area4 kept
0.90
Min-p · sets a floor4 kept
0.10
How sure is the model?

Flip between the two and watch the right-hand panel. Min‑p adapts — when the model is sure of itself the floor rises and almost nothing else survives; when it is torn the floor drops and the alternatives live. Top‑p cannot tell the difference.

02 — Where models come from

One site, one file format, a handful of packagers

Hugging Face

Where essentially every open model lives. A “repo” is a folder of files, not a product.

HUGGINGFACE.CO
GGUF

The GGUF file

One self-contained file: the weights plus tokenizer, and usually the chat template. This is what you download.

MLX USES ITS OWN FORMAT
WHO?

Who quantized it

Model authors rarely publish 4‑bit builds. Community packagers do.

BARTOWSKI · LMSTUDIO-COMMUNITY · MLX-COMMUNITY

The name in the search box is not the whole story. One model produces dozens of files at different quantizations — picking the right one is the skill.

02 — Under the hood

LM Studio is a wrapper. These do the work.

llama.cpp

The engine almost everything runs on. C++, no dependencies, runs on anything from a Raspberry Pi to a server. Reads GGUF.

EVERY PLATFORM

MLX

Apple’s own array framework, built for unified memory. Meaningfully faster than llama.cpp on a Mac, useless anywhere else.

APPLE SILICON ONLY

Worth knowing because it means the app is not the magic — it is a face on top of an engine, and you can change either one.

02 — Under the hood

If you outgrow LM Studio

Ollama

Terminal-first. One command pulls and runs a model, and it serves an API other apps can talk to.

OLLAMA RUN QWEN3

Open WebUI

A browser front end you self-host, usually pointed at Ollama. Multi-user, and closest to the hosted chat apps.

RUNS IN A BROWSER
G4A

GPT4All

The other friendly desktop app. Leans hard on chatting with your own documents.

DESKTOP APP

Same GGUF files underneath, so the model you just downloaded is not wasted — but moving is not quite free. Open WebUI is a front end and needs Ollama (or another server) behind it, and Ollama imports a local GGUF through a Modelfile rather than opening it directly.

03
Section 03

Hardware & the one formula

DRAM versus VRAM. Discrete GPU versus unified memory. And the single equation that explains every speed you will ever see.

03 — The one formula

Decode speed is a memory problem

tokens/sec ≈ memory bandwidthGB / SEC model sizeGB

The through-line of this entire workshop

Prefill
Reading your prompt
Every token of the prompt is processed at once. The chip is doing arithmetic flat out.
Limited by compute — FLOPS
Feels like: the pause before the first word
Decode
Writing the answer
One token at a time, and every weight in the model must be read from memory for each one.
Limited by memory bandwidth — GB/s
Feels like: the speed the words appear

A Mac has modest compute but wide memory, so it writes quickly and thinks slowly. A big discrete GPU is fast at both — right up until the model stops fitting in its VRAM.

This assumes the model fits. Drag the size past what the machine actually holds and the number above becomes a fantasy — that is the next slide. Even when it does fit, this is a theoretical ceiling: attention, sampling and the KV cache all take a cut, and no chip sustains its paper bandwidth.

03 — Prefill

Same two machines. Now watch who answers first.

Clock is real time · rates are estimates for one 8B at 4‑bit

The asymmetry The Mac is 2.2× behind on writing — and 11.6× behind on reading.

Prefill is arithmetic; decode is memory traffic. The 5090 has roughly three times the Mac's bandwidth but around five times its peak matrix compute — so which phase you are in decides how big the gap feels. The measured prefill gap is wider still, because llama.cpp's CUDA path is mature and its Metal path does not yet use the matrix units built into the M5 GPU (Apple calls them Neural Accelerators; they are not the separate Neural Engine, which no local runtime uses). Every rate here is an order‑of‑magnitude estimate for one 8 B model at 4‑bit, not a benchmark of your machine — only the clock is real. Attention is also quadratic, so a really long prompt is worse than this straight line suggests.

04 — What a quant actually is

Same weights. Fewer decimal places.

24 weights from one layer
Values it is allowed to be
Levels available
65,536
Average error
±0.0000
Bits per weight
16.00
A 30B model
60.0 GB
Why bother Smaller file → fits in memory you actually have. Half the bytes is twice the tokens per second — same formula as §3.

Note the shared scale. A quant does not store 24 tiny numbers — it stores 24 tiny integers plus one full-precision multiplier for the block. That multiplier is why a “4‑bit” file is never exactly 4 bits per weight, and real GGUF blocks carry more metadata than this one. Hold that thought for one slide.

Q4_K_M is 4.83 bits per weight, not 4. The gap between the two numbers above is the block scales from the last slide. Trust the napkin to tell you which models are plausible; trust the download page for the last gigabyte. The reserve assumes a short conversation — §5 is what happens to it when the conversation is long.

04 — Your turn

Same 15 GB. Same tokens per second. Which one do you download?

Bigger and more compressed usually wins. All three read 15 GB out of memory for every token, so all three decode at the same speed — bandwidth ÷ size does not care how the bytes are arranged. Size and speed are held constant, which leaves exactly one variable: how much model you got for the money.

Click an option to reveal — ask for hands first. The rule has a floor, and the floor is the next slide.

04 — The 4‑bit floor

Compression is nearly free — right up until it isn’t

4
bits per weight
30B model on disk
18.1 GB
Quality retained
98%

The sweet spot. Where almost everyone should live.

30B model 1–4B model

Small models fall further. A 30B has parameters to spare and shrugs off rounding; a 1B does not, which matters tonight because a 1B is what most of you downloaded. Below 4‑bit the failure is invisible — no error, no warning, just quiet loops, contradictions and confident nonsense. Shape of the curve: real. Exact percentages: illustrative, and they move with every model and benchmark.

Section 05

Context & the KV cache

Weights are fixed. The cache is not. Why a long conversation can run you out of memory that a short one never touched.

05 — The KV cache

It re-reads the whole conversation, and refuses to do it twice

2K and V× 32layers× 8KV heads× 128head dim× 2bytes = 128KB per token
Model
Attention
Cache
Per 1,000 tokens
0.13 GB
At 32k context
4.0 GB
Cache vs weights at 32k
0.8×
Memory against context length straight line, no surprises — that is the problem

GQA is why your arithmetic will over-estimate. The naive formula gives every attention head its own key and value; modern models share one KV head between groups of them, cutting the cache several-fold. Toggle it and watch the line pivot. Some models cut further still with sliding-window layers, which cap the cache instead of growing it.

This is why a million tokens is a hardware problem, not a setting. Drag to the far right: the cache dwarfs the model it belongs to, and no consumer machine holds it. Frontier providers do it with paged caches, aggressive KV quantization, sliding windows and racks of accelerators. On your laptop, the honest move is to set the context you actually need — LM Studio hands you that slider, and now you know what it costs.

Good at / bad at

First, honestly, how small the thing on your laptop is. Then why that matters far less than it sounds — for the right jobs.

06 — Sense of scale

Your laptop against the rest of the field

We are going to build this chart from the bottom up, starting with the model on your laptop.

Runs on a laptop Open weights, too big Closed weights Estimate, disputed Active per token

Nobody outside the lab knows the closed numbers. Open-weight vendors publish theirs; OpenAI, Anthropic and Google stopped in 2023. The white bars are inference, not fact — the two published attempts to measure them from the outside disagree by roughly six times, which is why they are drawn as ranges. The lesson survives the uncertainty: even the most conservative estimate is two orders of magnitude above anything you can hold in a laptop, and a sparse model only ever runs a small slice of that total at a time — the dot on each bar.

06 — Good at / bad at

A small model is a tool, not a smaller genius

Give it this
Not this

 

The pattern is one line: bring the knowledge to the model. Everything on the left hands it the material; everything on the right asks it to supply the material itself. That is why retrieval over your own files works far better than a 4 B model has any right to, and why “what do you know about …” disappoints. The right column is a difference of degree, not of kind — frontier models still hallucinate on 3–19% of fact-seeking questions depending on the model and the task, and error still compounds across a long run for everyone. A small model just reaches the edge sooner, and says nothing when it gets there.

Do not over‑read one number. A composite index compresses very different skills into a single score, its makeup changes between versions, and the 27 B still loses badly on exactly what §6 predicted — breadth of world knowledge, which is the thing parameters actually buy. OpenAI did not stand still either; the 2026 frontier is far above both bars here. The claim is only this: the line beneath you is rising fast, and it is rising in the open.

Sixteen bits per weight, exactly as the training run left it. Nothing on this slide is smarter than this row — it is only bigger.

16 GB laptop 8 GB laptop A phone

Bonsai (PrismML, Apache 2.0) is trained with {−1, 0, +1} weights from the start — never a 16‑bit model that got rounded, so there is nothing to lose on the way down: 8 B in 1.75 GB, benchmark average 75.5 against 70.5 for the earlier 1‑bit version that had no zero. The catch is real — its format is not in mainline llama.cpp, so it needs PrismML’s own fork or their MLX build, and will not appear in LM Studio tonight. Decode figures are §3’s formula on a published bandwidth, halved: PrismML measure 82 tok/s on an M4 Pro and 27 on an iPhone 17 Pro Max.

07 — Diffusion

What if it stopped writing left to right?

Both lanes at 2.5× slow motion · same slowdown, so the ratio on screen is the real one
Autoregressive Every model you ran tonight
0.00s
Per pass1 token Rate≈250 tok/s Passes0
Diffusion DiffusionGemma · Google DeepMind, Jun 2026
0.00s
Per pass256 tokens Rate>1,000 tok/s Passes0
Where the bottleneck went Autoregressive decode reads every weight once per token. Diffusion reads them once per block — so the memory bus stops being the wall, and arithmetic becomes it instead.

This is the formula from §3 breaking. tok/s ≈ bandwidth ÷ model size held all evening because one pass produced one token. Denoise 256 at a time and the same bus carries hundreds — which is why a Mac’s bandwidth advantage would matter less here, and raw compute more. The catch: DiffusionGemma is a 26 B mixture of experts with 3.8 B active, wants roughly 18 GB even quantized, scores below standard Gemma 4, and has no hosted API. Apache 2.0, weights on Hugging Face — and above tonight’s hardware ceiling. Rates are Google’s figures on a single H100, not on anything in this room.
